beats.say: Welcome to Advanced Models.
In this module, the model gets data with no labels, and has to discover the structure by itself.
In supervised learning, every example comes with the right answer, a label, like this photo is a cat.
In unsupervised learning, there are no labels. Imagine a box of five hundred mixed buttons, and nobody tells you the categories.
You'd sort them by colour, size or number of holes. That sorting is clustering: grouping similar items.
The second common job is finding associations: which things tend to happen together.
Dimensionality reduction, in Module 2, is a third.
K-means is the most popular clustering method. You choose k, the number of clusters, and it finds k centre points called centroids.
Start by picking k starting centroids, often k random data points.
Assign every point to its nearest centroid.
Update: move each centroid to the average position of its points.
Repeat until no point changes cluster. That's convergence. The goal is the smallest within-cluster sum of squared distances.
In the course, you can run K-means step by step in the lab.
K-means can get stuck in a poor answer depending on where it starts, so people run it several times.
It expects roughly round, similar-sized clusters.
And you choose k yourself. A common trick is the elbow method: plot the error for k equals one, two, three, and pick where the curve stops dropping sharply.
There are other families of clustering.
Centroid-based, like K-means: fast and simple, for round clusters.
Density-based, like D B SCAN: finds odd shapes, and labels lonely points as noise.
Hierarchical: builds a tree by merging or splitting groups, so you see clusters at many levels.
Distribution-based, like a Gaussian mixture model: soft, oval-shaped clusters, where each point gets a probability for every cluster.
And fuzzy, where points belong partly to several clusters. Don't confuse K-means with K-nearest-neighbours, which is supervised and needs labels.
Association rules find items that appear together, written X arrow Y: if X, then often Y.
Take ten baskets. Bread is in five, butter in three, and both together in three.
Support is three out of ten, point three. Confidence is three out of five, point six. Lift is point six divided by point three, which is two.
Lift above one means a real positive link. It corrects for how common Y already is. Try the rule calculator in the lab in the course.

scenes.title: What does K-means do in the update step?
options: Moves each centroid to the mean of its assigned points
scenes.good: That's right. Update means recomputing each centroid as the average of its points. Assign gives each point to its nearest centroid.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Update means recomputing each centroid as the average of its points. Assign gives each point to its nearest centroid.

beats.say: Quick check.
What does K-means do in the update step?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 1.
You're done when:
you can explain that unsupervised models discover structure without labels,
you can run K-means: assign, update, repeat,
you can match cluster shapes to methods like D B SCAN and Gaussian mixtures,
and you can score a rule with support, confidence and lift.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 2.
A three D object casts a two D shadow. Hold it at the right angle, and the shadow still shows most of its shape. Dimensionality reduction looks for that best angle.
Each feature is one measurement about an example. A small sixty-four by sixty-four grayscale image already has four thousand and ninety-six features.
Too many features cause trouble. Training is slower.
The data is hard to visualise.
And models can overfit, memorising noise. This is the curse of dimensionality.
Reducing helps, but some information is lost, and reducing too far hurts accuracy.
Feature selection keeps some of the original features and throws the rest away.
Filter methods score each feature on its own, like dropping features with low variance or high correlation.
Wrapper methods try subsets with a model, like forward selection or backward elimination.
Embedded methods let the model decide while training, like random forest feature importance.
Feature extraction builds new features by combining old ones. P C A is the classic example. Compact, but harder to interpret.
Principal component analysis finds new axes, called principal components, along the directions where the data spreads out most.
First, standardise each feature, so large-scale features don't dominate.
Second, compute the covariance matrix: how every pair of features varies together.
Third, find its eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Each eigenvector is a direction, and its eigenvalue says how much variance lies along it.
Fourth, keep the top k components and project the data onto them.
In the lab in the course, raise the correlation between two features, and watch almost all the spread line up along P C 1.

scenes.title: Explained variance
scenes.sub: explained variance of PCi = λi ÷ (λ1 + … + λn) · aim for 90–95%

beats.say: Each component's explained variance is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues.
Say the eigenvalues are four point two, one point one, point four and point three. The total is six.
So P C 1 explains seventy percent, and P C 2 eighteen percent. Keeping those two keeps eighty-eight percent of the variance with half the features.
A common rule: keep enough components to reach about ninety to ninety-five percent.

scenes.title: Eigenvalues are 6, 3 and 1. What share does PC1 explain?
scenes.good: That's right. Six divided by six plus three plus one is point six, so sixty percent.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Six divided by six plus three plus one is point six, so sixty percent.

beats.say: Quick check.
Eigenvalues are 6, 3 and 1. What share does PC1 explain?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 2.
You're done when:
you can say why too many features slow training and cause overfitting,
you can tell selection, which keeps original features, from extraction, which builds new ones,
you can follow P C A: standardise, covariance, eigenvectors, keep the top k,
and you can choose k with cumulative explained variance.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 3.
Classification gives one label for a whole image. Object detection finds every object, draws a box around each, and labels it.
YOLO, short for You Only Look Once, does it all in a single pass through one network, fast enough for real-time video.
YOLO divides the image into an S by S grid. The cell that contains an object's centre is responsible for detecting it.
Every cell predicts B boxes, each with five numbers: x, y, width, height and a confidence score. Plus C class probabilities.
So the output size is S times S times, five B plus C.
In the original YOLO, S is seven, B is two and C is twenty. That's thirty numbers per cell, and one thousand four hundred and seventy in total.
Try the grid in the lab in the course.
The image is resized to four hundred and forty-eight pixels square.
A backbone C N N with twenty-four convolutional layers and four max-pooling layers extracts features. It's first pre-trained on ImageNet classification.
Two fully connected layers turn those features into the one thousand four hundred and seventy predictions.
Leaky ReLU is used inside, a linear output at the end, and dropout reduces overfitting.
Training adds up squared errors for box position, confidence and class. Empty cells are down-weighted.
To judge a predicted box, compare it to the true box with intersection over union: area of overlap divided by area of union.
Two ten by ten boxes overlap in a five by ten strip. The overlap is fifty. The union is a hundred plus a hundred minus fifty, so one fifty.
I o U is fifty over one fifty, about point three three. One is a perfect match, and a detection usually counts as correct at point five or above.
In the I o U tab of the lab, you can drag a box and watch the number change.
Several boxes often fire on the same object. Non-maximum suppression removes the duplicates.
Throw away boxes below a confidence threshold.
Keep the most confident remaining box.
Delete every other box that overlaps it with I o U above a threshold, like point five.
Repeat with the next most confident box. Later YOLOs added anchor boxes and multi-scale predictions, but one fast pass stays the core idea.

scenes.title: Which grid cell is responsible for an object?
options: The cell containing the object's centre
scenes.good: That's right. Only the cell holding the object's centre predicts it, which avoids double counting.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Only the cell holding the object's centre predicts it, which avoids double counting.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which grid cell is responsible for an object?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 3.
You're done when:
you can explain detection as what plus where, in one network pass,
you can work out the output size, S times S times five B plus C,
you can compute I o U for two boxes,
and you can explain how non-maximum suppression removes duplicates.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 4.
Transformers were invented for text. The Vision Transformer, or ViT, makes an image look like a sentence of tokens.
Convolutional networks slide small filters across an image.
Layers stack up from edges, to textures, to parts, to objects.
They build in helpful assumptions: nearby pixels matter most, and a pattern means the same thing anywhere.
The downside: a filter only sees far-apart regions after many layers.
First, patchify: cut the image into equal, non-overlapping squares, like sixteen by sixteen pixels.
Each patch is flattened and multiplied by a learned matrix, giving a patch embedding.
The number of patches is height times width, divided by the patch size squared. A two twenty-four pixel image gives fourteen by fourteen, so one hundred and ninety-six patches.

ViT adds a learned positional embedding to each patch, because attention alone has no sense of order. And one extra C L S token at the front, whose final value the classifier uses. That's one hundred and ninety-seven tokens.
Try patchifying an image in the lab in the course.
Inside each block, every token looks at every other token and decides how much to borrow from each.
Each token makes a query: what am I looking for?
A key: what do I contain?
And a value: what will I pass on?
Attention is softmax of Q times K transposed, divided by the square root of d, times V. Softmax turns match scores into weights that add up to one.
Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. In the lab, click a patch to see one row of attention weights.
ViT stacks many identical blocks, twelve in ViT Base.
Each starts with LayerNorm, applied before each sub-layer for stable training.
Then multi-head self-attention, with a residual connection adding the input back.
Then a feed-forward network with a GELU activation, and another residual connection.
At the end, the C L S token goes through a small M L P head that outputs class probabilities.
C N Ns look at small local windows, build in locality, and work with less data.
ViT looks at all patches at once, learns from data, needs lots of it, and its cost grows with N squared.
Swin computes attention inside small windows, shifting them each layer so neighbours share information, and merges patches into a pyramid. Its cost grows with image size.
Tick Swin-style local windows in the lab to compare the number of attention pairs.

scenes.title: A 256 × 256 image with 32 × 32 patches gives how many patch tokens?
scenes.good: That's right. Two fifty-six divided by thirty-two is eight, and eight times eight is sixty-four.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Two fifty-six divided by thirty-two is eight, and eight times eight is sixty-four.

beats.say: Quick check.
A 256 × 256 image with 32 × 32 patches gives how many patch tokens?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 4.
You're done when:
you can turn an image into a sequence of patch tokens,
you can explain positional embeddings and the C L S token,
you can describe attention with queries, keys and values,
and you can compare C N Ns, ViT and Swin.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 5.
Most models so far were discriminative: given an image, predict a label. A generative model learns what the data itself looks like, so it can create new examples.
Uses include image synthesis, extra training data, filling in missing parts of images, and anomaly detection.

scenes.title: A forger and a detective
scenes.quote: Generator = art forger. Discriminator = detective. Goal: D(x) ≈ 0.5

beats.say: A generative adversarial network has two networks that compete.
The generator turns random noise into a fake sample. The discriminator outputs the probability that a sample is real.
Each time the detective catches a fake, the forger improves. Eventually the fakes are so good the detective can only guess: D of x is about point five.
Step one trains the discriminator. The generator makes fakes, and D sees real images labelled one and fakes labelled zero.
Compute D's loss and update only D.
Step two trains the generator. G makes new fakes, and its loss compares D's scores to the label it wants: one, real.
Backpropagate through D into G, and update only G. Repeat for many rounds.
GANs can be unstable, and can suffer mode collapse. In the course, the lab trains a tiny one D GAN live, so you can watch the two sides settle.
An autoencoder squeezes an input into a short code in the latent space, then a decoder rebuilds it.
A plain autoencoder maps each input to one exact point, which leaves gaps. Decode a random point and you may get nonsense.
A variational autoencoder's encoder outputs a mean, mu, and a spread, sigma. We sample z equals mu plus sigma times epsilon, where epsilon is random noise.
That's the reparameterisation trick. The randomness lives in epsilon, so we can still backpropagate through mu and sigma.

scenes.title: Two parts
items: Sharp but tricky · stable but blurrier

beats.say: The V A E loss has two parts.
Reconstruction loss: how different the output is from the input. It keeps outputs faithful.
K L divergence: how far each encoded cloud is from a standard normal. It keeps the latent space smooth, with no gaps.
To make something new, sample z from a standard normal and run the decoder. Try the V A E tab in the lab.
Compared with GANs, V A Es are stable with a smooth latent space, but often a little blurry. Today's leading image generators are diffusion models, which remove noise step by step.

scenes.title: What does the KL term in the VAE loss do?
options: Keeps the latent space close to N(0, 1) so it is smooth
scenes.good: That's right. It stops the encoder from scattering codes far apart, leaving no gaps.
scenes.bad: Not quite. It stops the encoder from scattering codes far apart, leaving no gaps.

beats.say: Quick check.
What does the KL term in the VAE loss do?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 5.
You're done when:
you can explain the generator versus discriminator game,
you can walk through one round of GAN training,
you can describe the encoder, latent space and decoder of a V A E,
and you can explain the reparameterisation trick and the two parts of the loss.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to the last module.
A large language model is a very large transformer trained on huge amounts of text. At its core it does one thing: predict the next token.
Repeat that over and over, and you get paragraphs, code and conversations.
First, tokenisation. Text is split into tokens. Unbelievable might become un, believ, able.
Then embeddings: each token becomes a vector, and words used in similar ways get similar vectors.
Then self-attention layers. In, the robot picked up the ball because it was light, attention helps it connect to ball.
Finally, a probability for every token in the vocabulary as the next one. Try it in the lab in the course.
Pre-training is self-supervised: the label is simply the next word in the text.
Then supervised fine-tuning, on example prompts paired with good answers, and instruction tuning, so it follows directions.
R L H F: people rank answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the L L M is tuned to score well.
Reasoning models get further reinforcement learning that rewards breaking hard problems into steps.

scenes.title: Temperature
scenes.sub: Low T → focused · High T → varied

beats.say: The model gives probabilities, and we pick a token from them. Temperature controls how adventurous that pick is.
Low temperature, like point two, almost always picks the top token: focused and repeatable.
High temperature, like one point five, gives more variety, and more risk. Top-k only allows the k most likely tokens.
Try both in the sampling tab of the lab.
Prompt engineering: clear instructions, context and examples get better answers.
The context window is the most tokens the model can read at once, your prompt plus its answer. Anything outside isn't seen.
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, searches your documents and places relevant passages in the context, so the model answers from up-to-date or private information without retraining.
Be careful: L L Ms can state wrong things confidently. That's hallucination. Check important claims.
Generative AI starts from a foundation model, trained on broad data.
Building an application has three phases: training the foundation model,
tuning it for a job, with fine-tuning, R L H F, or just good prompts and RAG,
and generating, evaluating and improving over time.
Multimodal models turn image patches into tokens, exactly as ViT does. That's how a model can describe a video frame.

scenes.title: You want the same, focused answer every time. Temperature should be…
scenes.good: That's right. Low temperature sharpens the probabilities towards the top token.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Low temperature sharpens the probabilities towards the top token.

beats.say: Quick check.
You want the same, focused answer every time. Temperature should be…
Tap your answer.
That's Module 6.
You're done when:
you can trace text from tokens to a next-token prediction,
you can explain self-attention in a sentence,
you can describe pre-training, fine-tuning and R L H F,
and you can use temperature, the context window and RAG correctly.
